item.content:encoded:
News / Benzinga / CoreWeave Has ‘Darwin Moment’ As Credit Markets Price In 60% Default Odds

CoreWeave Has ‘Darwin Moment’ As Credit Markets Price In 60% Default Odds 2 min read

CRWV NBIS For the AI infrastructure boom , the winning formula was to borrow heavily to build quickly. That strategy backfired on CoreWeave Inc. CRWV . Shares fell 6.4% to $65.25 by 9:40 a.m. ET on Friday, putting the stock on track for a weekly loss of about 22%. A close at that level would be its lowest since May 2025. CoreWeave’s five-year credit default swaps — contracts that insure investors against a missed debt payment — hit a record 1,194.5 basis points on Thursday, according to ICE Data Services data reported by Bloomberg. That price implies a more than 60% chance of default within five years, by standard market calculations. Its 9.75% notes due October 2031 slipped to 81.80 cents on the dollar on Friday, yielding 15.08%. Two months ago, the same bonds yielded about 12%.

Read Also: EXCLUSIVE: Is AI Growth Slowing Down? Memory Industry Expert Says It's 'Too Early' To Tell Why Higher Rates Hit CoreWeave First CoreWeave rents out Nvidia-powered computing capacity to AI developers. It buys the chips and builds the data centers before the rent arrives, and it borrows to fill the gap. In the second quarter, it generated $679 million in operating cash flow while spending about $6.4 billion on equipment. Net interest expense more than doubled to $640 million. That model worked when money was cheap. On Friday, the 10-year Treasury yield rose 4 basis points to 5.12%. The 30-year rose 3 basis points to 5.45%, and the 2-year held at 4.76%. Wednesday’s hotter-than-expected inflation report raised the odds of another Federal Reserve rate hike on Oct. 28. CoreWeave fell 15.5% that day. ‘Darwin Moment’ "Data centre bonds are having their Darwin moment, where the weakest credits struggle to survive," Ludovic Subran , chief investment officer at German insurer Allianz, told the Financial Times this week. Rival neocloud Nebius Group N.V. NBIS is down about 20% this week. Bank of America’s Michael Hartnett sees the pressure moving up the food chain. "We continue to lean risk-off next 3-4 weeks," the chief investment strategist said in his weekly Flow Show note. He cited 3% inflation-adjusted yields, the Nov. 3 midterms and weak trading in AI "spenders and lenders." The spenders are CoreWeave’s customers: Amazon , Alphabet , Meta , Microsoft and Oracle . The lenders include private credit firms, banks and bondholders. Their AI spending is expected to reach $807 billion this year. As a result, their combined free cash flow is forecast to swing from $191 billion in 2025 to minus $63 billion this year, according to consensus estimates compiled by Bank of America. Signal to Watch "A rollover in semi prices signals further tightening of AI credit," Hartnett said, expecting an October Fed hike to restore credibility. Consumer prices have run above the Fed’s 2% target for 66 consecutive months. In his view, a hike could pull long-term Treasury yields down another 20 basis points and limit losses in risky assets. The question now is which companies can afford to finance the AI race at elevated interest rates. item.title: Wall Street's Top Oil Bank Just Hit a Wall

item.content:encoded:
News / GuruFocus / Wall Street's Top Oil Bank Just Hit a Wall

Wall Street's Top Oil Bank Just Hit a Wall 2 min read

GS JPM MQG Macquarie's two-decade rise from an Australian lender to the world's top commodity bank is now facing a sharp reality check. Once rivaling Wall Street titans like Goldman Sachs GS and JPMorgan JPM , the firm's U.S. energy trading empire has started to lose its footing after the departure of longtime commodities chief Nick O'Kane, who joined Mercuria Energy Group in early 2024. His exit triggered a wave of high-profile departures across Houston's oil desk, halting crude exports and cutting natural gas trading volumes by 19%. Internal documents reviewed by Bloomberg show the bank was forced to amend nearly $600 million in government oil contracts as staff turnover and stricter compliance procedures slowed trading execution. What was once a high-octane profit engine now appears caught in a complex transition one shaped as much by regulation as by strategy. For years, Macquarie thrived on bold market bets and regulatory gaps that U.S. rivals couldn't exploit. The acquisitions of Cook Inlet Energy, Constellation Energy's gas trading arm, and Cargill's petroleum business gave it unmatched reach across energy markets, while its offshore structure shielded it from post-crisis constraints like Dodd-Frank. That edge allowed Macquarie to become a dominant player in U.S. natural gas and the top supplier of crude to the U.S. government, earning record profits during the 2022 energy shock. But momentum has faded. Net income from commodities dropped 19% in the fiscal year ended March 31, while shares slipped about 1% this year. By contrast, peers Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan have gained, suggesting investors are recalibrating expectations for a business that once delivered outsized returns from volatility. The new leadership team is now rewriting the playbook. Simon Wright, a 35-year veteran, has taken charge of the commodities division, while former Equinor executive Samuele Ravelli is steering an expanded push into liquefied natural gas a sector Macquarie views as its next growth frontier. The bank has shifted its North American trading arm into a non-banking entity to ease regulatory pressure and is emphasizing client-led trading over proprietary risk. Yet analysts say investor patience may be tested. The Americas still account for about 40% of Macquarie's commodities income, and the question hanging over the firm is whether its trading muscle can recover when markets turn or if this marks the end of Macquarie's era as the world's undisputed commodity powerhouse.
